gloss: vineyard; tend vines; planted garden-land, its fresh produce
summary: כֶּרֶם is a vineyard: a plot planted with vines, hedged and walled, with its tower and winepress (Isa 5:1–2), pruned, gathered and gleaned under the law (Lev 25:3; Deu 24:21), and held as a family’s inheritance (Num 16:14; 1Ki 21:3); once it is an olive plantation (Jdg 15:5). The verb is found only in the participle כֹּרְמִים, the vinedressers named with the farmers (Jol 1:11). כַּרְמֶל is planted, fruitful garden-land, set against wilderness and forest (Isa 32:15; Jer 4:26), and the fresh ears of new grain that Israel might not eat until the firstfruits sheaf was brought (Lev 23:14). Scripture makes the vineyard a picture of Israel, “the vineyard of Yahweh of Armies is the house of Israel” (Isa 5:7), which Jesus takes up in the parable of the vineyard let out to tenants (Mat 21:33–43); the vineyard is the word’s sense across the Semitic languages (Ugaritic, Phoenician, Aramaic, Arabic krm).

senses.definition: A plot of ground planted with vines and tended for their grapes and wine: planted, dug and cleared, hedged and walled, with a watch-tower, a booth and a winepress; pruned for six years and left the seventh, gathered and gleaned.

evidence.note: “My beloved had a כֶּרֶם on a very fruitful hill.”
He dug it, cleared its stones, planted it with a choice vine, built a tower in it and hewed out a winepress, and waited for grapes.
Noah, a man of the ground, planted a כֶּרֶם and drank of the wine (9:21).
“You will plant כְּרָמִים and work them, but you will not drink the wine nor gather the grapes.”
“Let us go early to the כְּרָמִים; let us see whether the vine has budded.”
In a neighbour’s כֶּרֶם one may eat grapes to the full, but put none in a vessel.
Six years you shall prune your כֶּרֶם.
In the sabbath year the כֶּרֶם is not pruned.
The seventh year’s rest is kept for the כֶּרֶם and the olive yard.
The כֶּרֶם is not stripped bare; the fallen grapes are left for the poor and the sojourner.
When you gather the grapes of your כֶּרֶם, you shall not glean it afterwards; it is for the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow.
A כֶּרֶם is not to be sown with two kinds of seed.
A man who has planted a כֶּרֶם and not yet used its fruit goes home from the battle.
A narrow path between the כְּרָמִים, a wall on this side and a wall on that.
Zion left like a booth in a כֶּרֶם.
The sluggard’s כֶּרֶם overgrown with thorns, its stone wall broken down (24:31).
Ten yoke of כֶּרֶם yield one bath of wine.
The Benjamites lie in wait in the כְּרָמִים at the dances of Shiloh.
David’s officers over the כְּרָמִים and over the wine cellars in them.
The little foxes that spoil the כְּרָמִים, for our כְּרָמִים are in blossom.

senses.definition: A vineyard as land owned and inherited, listed with field, olive yard and house as what a family lives by; to give vineyards is to give a livelihood, to take them is to take it away.

evidence.note: “You have not given us an inheritance of field and כֶּרֶם.”
Ahab asks for Naboth’s כֶּרֶם; Naboth answers that Yahweh forbid he should give the inheritance of his fathers (21:3).
Ahab goes down to the כֶּרֶם of Naboth to take possession of it.
The king “will take your fields and your כְּרָמִים and your olive yards, the best of them, and give them to his servants”.
“Will the son of Jesse give every one of you fields and כְּרָמִים?”
Houses, cisterns, כְּרָמִים and olive trees that you did not plant.
The people mortgage their fields, כְּרָמִים and houses to buy grain.
“Is it a time to take silver … olive yards and כְּרָמִים?”
“Houses and fields and כְּרָמִים will again be bought in this land.”
Nebuzaradan gives the poor of the land כְּרָמִים and fields.
The Rechabites were not to build a house, sow seed, nor plant or have a כֶּרֶם, but to dwell in tents.
Damage done by grazing in another man’s field or כֶּרֶם is repaid from the best of one’s own.

senses.definition: Once a planted grove of trees other than vines: כֶּרֶם זַיִת, an olive plantation.

evidence.note: Samson burns the shocks and the standing grain “and the כֶּרֶם זָיִת”.

senses.definition: The vineyard as a figure for the people Yahweh planted and tended, from whom he looked for fruit: the house of Israel and the men of Judah; also, in the Song, the beloved herself, her own vineyard.

evidence.note: “The כֶּרֶם of Yahweh of Armies is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah the planting of his delight; he looked for justice, and behold bloodshed.”
“Judge between me and my כֶּרֶם.”
“What more was there to do for my כֶּרֶם that I have not done?”
He will take away its hedge and break down its wall.
Yahweh enters into judgment with the elders and princes: “you have devoured the כֶּרֶם; the spoil of the poor is in your houses.”
“Many shepherds have destroyed my כֶּרֶם; they have trodden down my portion.”
“In that day: a כֶּרֶם of delight, sing of it!” Yahweh keeps it and waters it every moment (27:3).
Quoting Isa 5:2: a householder planted a vineyard, set a hedge about it, dug a winepress and built a tower, and let it out to tenants.
“They made me keeper of the כְּרָמִים; my own כֶּרֶם I have not kept.”
“My כֶּרֶם, which is mine, is before me.”
Solomon’s כֶּרֶם at Baal-hamon, let out to keepers for a thousand pieces of silver for its fruit.

senses.definition: One who works the vineyards, named beside the farmer who works the fields: the poor of the land left by Babylon to keep the land producing, the vinedressers of Uzziah, the foreigners who will work Israel’s land.

evidence.note: “Be ashamed, farmers; wail, כֹּרְמִים”, for the harvest of the field has perished and the vine is dried up (1:12).
The captain of the guard leaves some of the poor of the land as כֹּרְמִים and farmers.
Sons of the foreigner will be Israel’s farmers and כֹּרְמִים.
Uzziah had farmers and כֹּרְמִים in the hills and in the כַּרְמֶל, for he loved the ground.
The ἀμπελουργός of the parable of the fig tree in the vineyard.

words.gloss: planted garden-land, fruitful land; fresh ears of grain
words.summary: Planted, fruitful land, the opposite of wilderness and of forest, where vineyards and gardens grow (Isa 16:10 sets it beside the vineyards and winepresses); in Lev 2:14, 23:14 and 2Ki 4:42, the fresh ears of the new grain. How the fresh grain comes from the garden-land is not clear: perhaps as its new produce. The same word is the name of Mount Carmel and of a town in Judah, both places of good pasture (Jer 50:19; 1Sa 25:2), which are not entered here.

senses.definition: Land planted and fruitful, with vineyards, gardens and trees: what the wilderness becomes when Yahweh restores it, and what becomes wilderness under his judgment; it ranks between the wild forest and the barren wilderness.

evidence.note: When the Spirit is poured out from on high, the wilderness becomes כַּרְמֶל and the כַּרְמֶל is counted a forest.
Justice dwells in the wilderness and righteousness abides in the כַּרְמֶל.
Lebanon turns into כַּרְמֶל, and the כַּרְמֶל is counted a forest.
“I looked, and behold, the כַּרְמֶל was the wilderness, and all its cities broken down.”
“I brought you into a land of כַּרְמֶל, to eat its fruit and its good.”
Gladness and joy are taken from the כַּרְמֶל; in the vineyards no singing, no treader treads wine in the presses.
The same lament for Moab: gladness taken from the כַּרְמֶל and wine from the presses.
The glory of the Assyrian’s forest and his כַּרְמֶל consumed.
Sennacherib boasts he reached Lebanon’s farthest lodge, “the forest of its כַּרְמֶל”.
Uzziah’s vinedressers in the hills and in the כַּרְמֶל; the garden-land or the place Carmel.
Israel dwelling alone, “a forest in the midst of כַּרְמֶל”; the garden-land or Mount Carmel.

senses.definition: The new grain of the harvest, eaten fresh or crushed from the ripe ears: brought as the grain offering of firstfruits, and not to be eaten, with bread and roasted grain, until the day the firstfruits sheaf was brought to Yahweh.

evidence.note: “Bread, roasted grain and כַּרְמֶל you shall not eat until this same day, until you have brought the offering of your God.”
The grain offering of firstfruits: green ears roasted with fire, גֶּרֶשׂ כַּרְמֶל, grain crushed from the fresh ears.
A man brings the man of God bread of the firstfruits, twenty barley loaves, and כַּרְמֶל in his sack.

opposites.note: Wilderness becomes garden-land in restoration, and garden-land wilderness in judgment.
Set against the wild forest: Lebanon becomes garden-land, garden-land is counted forest.

phrases.gloss: a land of garden-land, a fruitful land
grain crushed from the fresh ears

words.summary: A late word for crimson-dyed stuff, found only in Chronicles, where Exodus has תּוֹלַעַת שָׁנִי, “worm of scarlet”. It is very likely not of this root: Arabic قِرْمِز, the kermes dye, comes from the Indo-Iranian word for “worm”, and כַּרְמִיל from the same word; its likeness to כֶּרֶם is of sound only. It is kept here because the text files it under this spelling, until it has an entry of its own.

senses.definition: Cloth or yarn dyed deep red, worked with blue, purple and fine linen in the temple’s veil and hangings.

evidence.note: The veil of blue, purple, כַּרְמִיל and fine linen, with cherubim worked on it, as the veil of Exo 26:31 is of blue, purple, תּוֹלַעַת שָׁנִי and fine twined linen.
The tabernacle veil, whose colours 2Ch 3:14 repeats with כַּרְמִיל for תּוֹלַעַת שָׁנִי.
Solomon asks Hiram for a man skilled in purple, כַּרְמִיל and blue.
Huram-abi, skilled in purple, blue, fine linen and כַּרְמִיל.

cognates.note: Egyptian has the vineyard (later written kꜣm) and the gardener or vintner with the same consonants, as Hebrew has כֶּרֶם and כֹּרֵם; Coptic keeps both, ϭⲱⲙ “garden, vineyard, property” (Comprehensive Coptic Lexicon C7724) and ϭⲙⲉ “gardener, vinedresser, wine grower” (C7725). That the word passed between Egyptian and the Semitic languages is likely; which way it went is not shown, and the Semitic word is old and widespread (Ugarit, Phoenicia, Arabia, Ethiopia).

doctrine.statement: Isaiah sings of a vineyard its owner dug, cleared, planted with a choice vine, guarded with a tower and furnished with a winepress, and which gave only wild grapes; he will take away its hedge and leave it waste, and he explains: “the vineyard of Yahweh of Armies is the house of Israel … he looked for justice, and behold bloodshed” (Isa 5:1–7). Yahweh enters into judgment with the elders and princes because they “have devoured the vineyard” (Isa 3:14), and “many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard” (Jer 12:10). Jesus told the chief priests and elders of a householder who planted a vineyard in the words of Isa 5:2, let it out to tenants, and sent servants and at last his son, whom they killed; they themselves answered that he would destroy those men and give the vineyard to others, and he said, “the kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation bringing forth its fruits”, and they knew he spoke of them (Mat 21:33–45). From the verses: the vineyard is the people, the tenants are their rulers, the fruit Yahweh looks for is justice and righteousness, and the son is Jesus; the tenants’ end came when Jerusalem’s rulers and their city were destroyed in AD 70, within that generation (Mat 23:36–38). Yet Isaiah also sings of the vineyard “in that day”, kept and watered by Yahweh, when Israel will blossom and fill the face of the world with fruit (Isa 27:2–6).

Israel received vineyards it had not planted (Deu 6:11; Jos 24:13). The covenant’s curse is to plant a vineyard and not use it, to plant vineyards and not drink their wine (Deu 28:30, 39), and the prophets turn it on those who trampled the poor (Amo 5:11; Zep 1:13). The promise of restoration is the reverse: “they will plant vineyards and drink their wine” (Amo 9:14), on the mountains of Samaria (Jer 31:5), dwelling securely when Yahweh has judged their neighbours (Ezk 28:26); and in the new heavens and new earth Yahweh creates, with Jerusalem a rejoicing, “they will plant vineyards and eat their fruit; they will not plant and another eat” (Isa 65:17–22). From the verses: whether Israel eats the fruit of its own vineyards follows its faithfulness to the covenant, and the age to come is pictured as a people settled on the land, eating what they planted, in a kingdom on the earth.

Israel might eat no bread, roasted grain or כַּרְמֶל, the fresh ears of the new harvest, until it had brought the sheaf of the firstfruits to the priest, who waved it before Yahweh “on the morrow after the sabbath” (Lev 23:10–14). The women came to Jesus’ tomb as the sabbath ended, toward the first day of the week, and found him risen (Mat 28:1–6); Paul writes, “now Christ is risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep … Christ the firstfruits, afterward those who are Christ’s at his coming” (1Co 15:20, 23). From the verses: the first of the harvest belonged to Yahweh before any of it was eaten, and Christ, raised on the morrow after the sabbath, is that first sheaf, the pledge of the harvest of his people at his return.

note: Drafted 2026-11-13. Root key כרמ, as the corpus keys it. bdb: k.dd.aa (כֶּרֶם), k.dd.ab (the participle כֹּרְמִים), k.dd.ae (כַּרְמֶל, the common noun), k.dd.ah (כַּרְמִיל). Token counts: the corpus maps BDB keys by spelling, so k.dd.ae (31) and the place k.dd.af (33) each hold most of the other’s tokens: of k.dd.ae’s, Jos 12:22, 15:55, 1Sa 25:2, 25:7, 1Ki 18:19–42, 2Ki 2:25, 4:25, Isa 33:9, 35:2, Jer 50:19, Amo 1:2, 9:3 are the place; k.dd.aa holds Num 26:6, Jos 7:1, 7:18 and 1Ch 2:7, which are Carmi, and Jer 6:1 and Neh 3:14, which are the place בֵּית הַכֶּרֶם. Left out: the places Carmel (k.dd.af; the mountain and the town of Judah, Jos 15:55, 1Sa 25) and Beth-haccherem, which cannot be name entries; the gentilics כַּרְמְלִי “Carmelite” (k.dd.ag: Nabal, Abigail, Hezro) and כַּרְמִי “Carmite” (k.dd.ad, Num 26:6), left with the names; the name כַּרְמִי Carmi (k.dd.ac; Reuben’s son and Achan’s father), not written, since the task gave no names; כְּרָן Keran (k.dd.ai, Gen 36:26; 1Ch 1:41), an Edomite whose consonants are כרן, filed here by BDB only, and not of this root. k.dd.aj is a cross-reference to כסם. Arabic كرم “be noble, generous, precious” (Lane p. 2999; Krahmalkov’s Punic K-R-M I “honour”) is not recorded as a cognate: no Hebrew word of the root means it. Open: (1) כַּרְמִיל is kept in the entry because the corpus files it here, though the evidence (Arabic qirmiz, Persian, “worm”) puts it under another root; move it to an entry of its own if the reviewer agrees. (2) Song 7:6 “your head upon you like כַּרְמֶל, and the hair of your head like purple” is filed as the mountain; the parallel with purple (אַרְגָּמָן) would suit כַּרְמִיל “crimson”, but the text spells כַּרְמֶל, so it is not cited. (3) The link between garden-land and “fresh ears” (Lev 2:14; 23:14; 2Ki 4:42) is not shown by any cognate; Lane’s “land yielding increase of its seed-produce” is the nearest, named on the word as a whole. (4) Mic 7:14 and 2Ch 26:10: garden-land or the place Carmel; cited under garden-land as examples only. (5) The AD 70 reading in the vineyard doctrine and the morrow-after-the-sabbath reading in firstfruits-first are stated as the conclusions; review. Not consulted: CAD K for karānu; Dillmann and Leslau for Ge’ez; Payne Smith for Syriac ܟܪܡܐ “vinedresser”; DULAT for Ugaritic krm.
